# Part A: Inversion

## A.1

The generator
$$x_{k+1} = 65539\, x_k \bmod 2^{31}, \qquad u_k = x_k / 2^{31},$$
is called RANDU.

Write `randu(seed, n)`, which returns $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ starting from
$x_0 = {}$`seed`. The mod operator in R is `%%`.

```{r}
randu_one <- function(seed) {
  (65539 * seed) %% 2^31
}

randu_ints <- function(seed, n) {
  xs <- numeric(n)
  for (i in 1:n) {
    seed <- randu_one(seed)
    xs[i] <- seed
  }
  xs
}
```


(a) Print $x_1, \ldots, x_{10}$ for seed 406. What do all ten have in common?

```{r}
options(digits = 22)
randu_ints(406, 10)
```

They are all even, realistically 50% should be odd. Depending on the seed, every
number will either be even or odd.

(b) Make a QQ plot of $u_1, \ldots, u_{30000}$ against $U(0, 1)$.

```{r}
randu <- function(seed, n) {
  xs <- randu_ints(seed, n)
  xs / 2^31
}

u30k <- randu(406, 30000)

ggplot(tibble(u = u30k),
       aes(sample = u)) +
  geom_qq(distribution = qunif) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color= "red")
```


(c) The function below groups draws into consecutive triples
$(u_1, u_2, u_3), (u_4, u_5, u_6), \ldots$ and plots them as points in the
unit cube. Run it on your 30,000 RANDU draws and on 30,000 draws from
`runif`. How do the two plots differ?

```{r plot-triples}
plot_triples <- function(u) {
  m <- matrix(u, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
  colnames(m) <- c("x", "y", "z")
  lattice::cloud(z ~ x + y, data = as.data.frame(m), pch = 20, cex = 0.1)
}

plot_triples(u30k)
plot_triples(runif(30000))
```

## A.2

`airquality$Wind` holds 153 daily average wind speeds (mph) at LaGuardia
Airport, May to September 1973. We model wind speed with the **log-logistic**
distribution, which has scale $\alpha > 0$, shape $\beta > 0$ and CDF
$$F(x) = \frac{1}{1 + (x / \alpha)^{-\beta}}, \qquad x > 0.$$
R has no functions for this distribution.

(a) Find the quantile function $Q(u)$, and write `rllogis(n, alpha, beta)`.
Check 10,000 draws with $\alpha = 10$ and $\beta = 5$ with a QQ plot against
your $Q$, as in video 1. `geom_qq` passes extra parameters to the quantile
function through `dparams`, for example
`geom_qq(distribution = qllogis, dparams = list(alpha = 10, beta = 5))`.

$$F(x) = \frac{1}{(1+x/\alpha)^{-\beta}} = u$$

$$Q(u) = \alpha(\frac{u}{1 - u})^{1/\beta}$$
```{r}
# Define the quantile function for the Log-Logistic distribution
qllogis <- function(p, alpha, beta) {
  alpha * (p / (1 - p))^(1 / beta)
}

# Define the inversion random number generator
rllogis <- function(n, alpha, beta) {
  u <- runif(n)
  qllogis(u, alpha, beta)
}

# Generate 10,000 draws with alpha = 10 and beta = 5
draws_llogis <- rllogis(10000, alpha = 10, beta = 5)

# Create the Q-Q plot against theoretical quantiles
ggplot(tibble(x = draws_llogis), aes(sample = x)) +
  geom_qq(distribution = qllogis, dparams = list(alpha = 10, beta = 5)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, color = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Q-Q Plot of rllogis Draws vs. Theoretical Log-Logistic Quantiles",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


(b) The method of moments (module 1) estimates parameters by setting the
model's moments equal to the sample's and solving. **Quantile matching** does
the same with quantiles. With $\hat q_p$ the sample $p$ quantile
(`quantile(x, p)`), solve
$$Q(1/2) = \hat q_{0.5}, \qquad Q(3/4) = \hat q_{0.75}$$
for $\alpha$ and $\beta$. This gives the estimators $\hat\alpha$ and
$\hat\beta$. Hint: start with $Q(1/2)$, then divide the second equation by
the first.
Compute them for the wind data. Then compare the fitted model's
probability of a day above 15 mph with the fraction of days above 15 mph in
the data.

$$Q(0.5) = \alpha \left( \frac{0.5}{1 - 0.5} \right)^{1/\beta} = \alpha (1)^{1/\beta} = \alpha \implies \hat{\alpha} = \hat{q}_{0.5}$$

$$Q(0.75) = \alpha \left( \frac{0.75}{1 - 0.75} \right)^{1/\beta} = \alpha (3)^{1/\beta} = \hat{q}_{0.75}$$

$$\frac{\hat{q}_{0.75}}{\hat{q}_{0.5}} = 3^{1/\beta}$$

$$\log\left(\frac{\hat{q}_{0.75}}{\hat{q}_{0.5}}\right) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log(3) \implies \hat{\beta} = \frac{\log(3)}{\log(\hat{q}_{0.75} / \hat{q}_{0.5})}$$

```{r}
# Extract wind speed data (153 daily observations)
wind_data <- airquality$Wind

# Compute sample quantiles
q50 <- quantile(wind_data, 0.50)
q75 <- quantile(wind_data, 0.75)

# Compute parameter estimates
hat_alpha <- as.numeric(q50)
hat_beta <- as.numeric(log(3) / log(q75 / q50))

cat(sprintf("Fitted alpha (scale): %.4f\n", hat_alpha))
cat(sprintf("Fitted beta  (shape): %.4f\n\n", hat_beta))

# Model probability of a day exceeding 15 mph: P(X > 15) = 1 - F(15)
# F(x) = 1 / (1 + (x / alpha)^(-beta))
model_prob_gt15 <- 1 - (1 / (1 + (15 / hat_alpha)^(-hat_beta)))

# Sample fraction of days exceeding 15 mph
sample_frac_gt15 <- mean(wind_data > 15)

cat(sprintf("Model probability P(X > 15): %.4f\n", model_prob_gt15))
cat(sprintf("Sample fraction  P(X > 15): %.4f\n", sample_frac_gt15))
```

(c) Simulate 1,000 samples of size 153 from the fitted model. Estimate the
bias and MSE of $\hat\beta$, each with a 99% confidence interval.

```{r}
# Parameter values from Part A.2(b)
alpha_true <- as.numeric(quantile(airquality$Wind, 0.50))
beta_true <- as.numeric(log(3) / log(quantile(airquality$Wind, 0.75) / alpha_true))

M <- 1000
n <- 153

beta_hats <- numeric(M)

for (i in 1:M) {
  # 1. Simulate a sample of size n from the log-logistic model
  sample_x <- rllogis(n, alpha_true, beta_true)
  
  # 2. Re-estimate beta via quantile matching
  q50_sim <- quantile(sample_x, 0.50)
  q75_sim <- quantile(sample_x, 0.75)
  
  beta_hats[i] <- as.numeric(log(3) / log(q75_sim / q50_sim))
}

# --- Point Estimates ---
bias_hat <- mean(beta_hats) - beta_true
mse_hat <- mean((beta_hats - beta_true)^2)

# --- 99% Confidence Intervals ---
# 1. CI for Bias: bias_hat +/- z_0.005 * SE(bias)
se_bias <- sd(beta_hats) / sqrt(M)
z_99 <- qnorm(0.995)

ci_bias <- bias_hat + c(-1, 1) * z_99 * se_bias

# 2. CI for MSE: using sample standard deviation of squared errors
sq_errors <- (beta_hats - beta_true)^2
se_mse <- sd(sq_errors) / sqrt(M)

ci_mse <- mse_hat + c(-1, 1) * z_99 * se_mse

# --- Display Output ---
cat(sprintf("True Beta: %.4f\n\n", beta_true))

cat(sprintf("Estimated Bias: %.4f\n", bias_hat))
cat(sprintf("99%% CI for Bias: [%.4f, %.4f]\n\n", ci_bias[1], ci_bias[2]))

cat(sprintf("Estimated MSE : %.4f\n", mse_hat))
cat(sprintf("99%% CI for MSE : [%.4f, %.4f]\n", ci_mse[1], ci_mse[2]))
```


## A.3

`discoveries` counts the great inventions and scientific discoveries in each
year from 1860 to 1959.

```{r discoveries}
d <- as.numeric(discoveries)
table(d)
```

(a) The Poisson($\lambda$) PMF is
$$p(x) = \frac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots,$$
which `dpois(x, lambda)` computes. Write `rpois_inv(n, lambda)`, which draws
Poisson($\lambda$) values by inversion: tabulate the CDF
$F(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{x} p(i)$, then for each $u$ find the smallest
$x$ with $F(x) \ge u$. Do not use `rpois` or `qpois`. Check 10,000 draws with
$\lambda = 3.1$ against `dpois(0:10, 3.1)`.

```{r}
# Custom Poisson generator via Inversion
rpois_inv <- function(n, lambda) {
  # Choose a safe upper bound M for CDF tabulation (lambda + 10 * sqrt(lambda))
  max_x <- ceiling(lambda + 10 * sqrt(lambda) + 20)
  
  # Tabulate PMF and CDF
  pmf <- dpois(0:max_x, lambda)
  cdf <- cumsum(pmf)
  
  # Draw uniforms and invert via interval matching
  u <- runif(n)
  findInterval(u, cdf) # Returns 0-indexed count x
}

# Check 10,000 draws with lambda = 3.1
set.seed(20260929)
n_draws <- 10000
lam <- 3.1
draws_pois <- rpois_inv(n_draws, lam)

# Compare sample probabilities against theoretical PMF dpois(0:10, 3.1)
observed_props <- prop.table(table(factor(draws_pois, levels = 0:10)))
theoretical_pmf <- dpois(0:10, lam)

comparison_df <- tibble(
  x = 0:10,
  Theoretical = theoretical_pmf,
  Sample = as.numeric(observed_props)
)

print(comparison_df)
```


(b) A Poisson variable has variance equal to its mean, so for Poisson counts
$S^2 / \bar X$ should be near 1. Compute it for `discoveries`. Simulate its
null distribution from 5,000 samples of size 100 drawn with `rpois_inv` at
$\lambda = \bar X$, and report the Monte Carlo $p$-value for the alternative
that the variance exceeds the mean.

```{r}
d <- as.numeric(discoveries)
n_obs <- length(d)

# Observed statistic
xbar_obs <- mean(d)
s2_obs <- var(d)
T_obs <- s2_obs / xbar_obs

# Simulate null distribution from 5,000 samples of size 100
M_sims <- 5000
T_sims <- numeric(M_sims)

set.seed(20260929)
for (i in 1:M_sims) {
  sim_sample <- rpois_inv(n_obs, lambda = xbar_obs)
  T_sims[i] <- var(sim_sample) / mean(sim_sample)
}

# Monte Carlo p-value for the upper-tailed test
p_value <- mean(T_sims >= T_obs)

cat(sprintf("Observed Mean (Xbar): %.4f\n", xbar_obs))
cat(sprintf("Observed Variance (S^2): %.4f\n", s2_obs))
cat(sprintf("Observed Dispersion Ratio (S^2 / Xbar): %.4f\n\n", T_obs))
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo p-value (H1: Variance > Mean): %.4f\n", p_value))
```


# Part B: Transformations and mixtures

## B.1

Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent $N(0, 1)$, and write the point $(X, Y)$ in
polar coordinates: radius $R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}$ and angle $A$, so that
$X = R \cos A$ and $Y = R \sin A$.

(a) Show that $R^2$ is exponential with rate $1/2$. You may use that
$\chi^2(2)$ is the exponential distribution with mean 2.

The square of a Normal RV follows a chi-squared distribution with one degree
of freedom. Sum of squares adds degrees of freedom $\chi^2(2)$. Using
the PDF of chi-squared gives us $(1/2)e^((-1/2))v$ which is exp(1/2).

(b) Take as given that $A \sim U(0, 2\pi)$, independent of $R$. Use the
exponential quantile function from video 1 to show that for independent
$U_1, U_2 \sim U(0, 1)$,
$$\sqrt{-2 \log U_1} \, \cos(2 \pi U_2) \sim N(0, 1).$$

- We know (a), that $R^2 \sim \text{Exp}(1/2)$
- How could we generate $R^2 = W$? If we know the quantile function $W$ 
is $-2 \log(1 - u)$, so to generate $W$ we draw $U_1 \sim U(0,1)$ and
$$-2 \log(1 - U_1) \sim \text{Exp}(1/2)$$ 
also $1 - U_1$ is uniform so:
$$-2 \log(1 - U_1) \sim \text{Exp}(1/2)$$ 

Conclude $R = \sqrt{-2 \log U_1}$

Now how to get $A$? From Inversion Method Lecture,
A's quantile function is $Q_A(u) = 2 \pi u$, so
$2 \pi U_2 = A$

Combined: $\sqrt{-2 \log U_1} \times \cos(2 \pi U_2)$
$= X \sim N(0,1)$


(c) Implement this as `rnorm_bm(n)`. Check 10,000 draws with a QQ plot, and
estimate $P(X > 2)$ with a 95% confidence interval. Compare with `pnorm(-2)`.

```{r}
# Function to generate standard normal draws using Box-Muller
rnorm_bm <- function(n) {
  m <- ceiling(n / 2)
  u1 <- runif(m)
  u2 <- runif(m)
  
  r <- sqrt(-2 * log(u1))
  theta <- 2 * pi * u2
  
  x1 <- r * cos(theta)
  x2 <- r * sin(theta)
  
  # Return exactly n samples
  c(x1, x2)[1:n]
}

# Generate 10,000 draws
draws <- rnorm_bm(10000)

# 1. Check distributional fit with a QQ plot
qqnorm(draws, main = "Q-Q Plot of rnorm_bm Draws")
qqline(draws, col = "red", lwd = 2)

# 2. Estimate P(X > 2) and compute a 95% Confidence Interval
p_hat <- mean(draws > 2)
n_obs <- length(draws)
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n_obs)

ci_lower <- p_hat - 1.96 * se
ci_upper <- p_hat + 1.96 * se

# 3. Theoretical value P(X > 2) = P(X < -2) = pnorm(-2)
p_true <- pnorm(-2)

# Print results
cat(sprintf("Estimated P(X > 2): %.4f\n", p_hat))

cat(sprintf("95%% CI: [%.4f, %.4f]\n", ci_lower, ci_upper))

cat(sprintf("Theoretical P(X > 2) [pnorm(-2)]: %.4f\n", p_true))
```

## B.2

A **zero-inflated Poisson** (ZIP) is zero with some extra probability and
otherwise Poisson. With a latent $W \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\theta)$
independent of $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$, let $Y = WX$.

(a) Write `rzip(n, theta, lambda)` from this representation. Use `rpois` for
$X$.

```{r}
rzip <- function(n, theta, lambda) {
  w <- rbinom(n, size=1, prob=theta)
  x <- rpois(n, lambda)
  w * x
}
```


(b) The method of moments estimators are
$$\hat \lambda = \frac{S^2 + \bar Y^2}{\bar Y} - 1, \qquad
  \hat \theta = 1 - \frac{S^2 - \bar Y}{S^2 + \bar Y^2 - \bar Y}.$$
Fit the ZIP to `discoveries`. How many of the 100 years does the fitted model
expect to have no discoveries, and how many did?

```{r}
d <- as.numeric(discoveries)
n_obs <- length(d)

# Sample moments
y_bar <- mean(d)
s2 <- var(d)

# Method of Moments Estimators
hat_lambda <- (s2 + y_bar^2) / y_bar - 1
hat_theta  <- 1 - (s2 - y_bar) / (s2 + y_bar^2 - y_bar)

# Model's expected probability of zero count: P(Y = 0) = theta + (1 - theta) * exp(-lambda)
p_zero_fitted <- hat_theta + (1 - hat_theta) * exp(-hat_lambda)

# Expected zero counts out of 100 years
expected_zeros <- n_obs * p_zero_fitted

# Actual observed zeros
observed_zeros <- sum(d == 0)

cat(sprintf("Fitted Lambda : %.4f\n", hat_lambda))
cat(sprintf("Fitted Theta  : %.4f\n\n", hat_theta))

cat(sprintf("Expected Zeros (Model) : %.2f years\n", expected_zeros))
cat(sprintf("Observed Zeros (Data)  : %d years\n", observed_zeros))
```


(c) Simulate 2,000 samples of size 100 from the fitted ZIP, and give a Monte
Carlo $p$-value for the observed number of zeros. The alternative is that
there are fewer zeros than the model predicts.

```{r}
M_sims <- 2000
sim_zeros <- numeric(M_sims)

# Simulate 2,000 samples of size 100 from the fitted ZIP model
for (i in 1:M_sims) {
  sim_data <- rzip(100, theta = hat_theta, lambda = hat_lambda)
  sim_zeros[i] <- sum(sim_data == 0)
}

# Monte Carlo p-value for the alternative: fewer zeros than predicted
p_value_zeros <- mean(sim_zeros <= observed_zeros)

cat(sprintf("Observed Zeros: %d\n", observed_zeros))
cat(sprintf("Mean Simulated Zeros: %.2f\n", mean(sim_zeros)))
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo p-value (H1: fewer zeros than predicted): %.4f\n", p_value_zeros))
```


# Part C: Accept-reject and importance resampling

The standard Laplace density is $g(x) = \frac{1}{2} e^{-|x|}$. Video 3 samples
it by inversion:

```{r rlaplace}
rlaplace <- function(n) {
  u <- runif(n)
  ifelse(u < 1/2, log(2 * u), -log(2 - 2 * u))
}
```

## C.1

(a) Find with pen and paper the smallest $c$ such that $c \, g(x) \ge \phi(x)$
for all $x$, where $\phi$ is the standard normal density. Treat $x \ge 0$ and
$x < 0$ separately.

$$\log \frac{e^{-x^2/2}/ \sqrt{2\pi}}{(1/2)e^{-x}} = \log
\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot e^{-x^{2}/2 + x} \right)$$

$$\log (2/\sqrt{2\pi)} + \log (e^{-x^{2}/2 + x})$$

$$\log (2/\sqrt{2\pi)} + \frac{-x^2}{2}+x$$

Derivative: $$-x+1$$

$c = \phi(x)/g(x)$? $$\frac{2e^{1/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{2e}{\pi}} = ~1.3155$$

(b) Use accept-reject with 10,000 Laplace candidates to draw standard
normals. Check the accepted draws with a QQ plot. Report the acceptance rate
with a 95% confidence interval, and compare it with $1/c$.

```{r c1b}
c_lap <- sqrt(2 * exp(1) / pi)                  # in R, e is exp(1)
y <- rlaplace(10000)
keep <- runif(10000) <= dnorm(y) / (c_lap * (exp(-abs(y)) / 2))   # c times g(y)
z <- y[keep]

# your QQ plot of z here
ggplot(tibble(z), aes(sample = z)) + geom_qq(distribution=qnorm) + 
  geom_abline(intercept=0,slope=1,color="red")

mean(keep)                          # acceptance rate
1 / c_lap
t.test(as.numeric(keep))$conf.int   # 95% interval for the acceptance rate
```

## C.2

Let $f(x) \propto f^*(x) = \sin(\pi x^2)$ on $0 < x < 1$. Neither method
below needs the normalizing constant.

```{r fstar}
fstar <- function(x) sin(pi * x^2)
curve(fstar(x), from = 0, to = 1)
```

(a) Use accept-reject with a $U(0, 1)$ envelope and 10,000 candidates. Since
$f^* \le 1$, accept a candidate $Y$ when $U \le f^*(Y)$.

```{r}
fstar <- function(x) sin(pi * x^2)

# --- (a) Accept-Reject Sampler using a U(0, 1) Envelope ---
set.seed(20260929)

n_target_ar <- 10000
ar_draws <- numeric(n_target_ar)
count <- 0
total_candidates <- 0

while (count < n_target_ar) {
  y <- runif(1)
  total_candidates <- total_candidates + 1
  
  # Accept candidate Y if U <= f*(Y) / envelope (envelope = 1)
  if (runif(1) <= fstar(y)) {
    count <- count + 1
    ar_draws[count] <- y
  }
}

# Acceptance rate check
ar_acc_rate <- n_target_ar / total_candidates
cat(sprintf("Accept-Reject Acceptance Rate: %.2f%%\n", ar_acc_rate * 100))
```


(b) Use importance resampling. Draw 10,000 new $U(0, 1)$ candidates, normalize
the weights $f^*(Y_i)$, and resample 5,000 draws with
`sample(..., replace = TRUE, prob = ...)`.

```{r}
# --- (b) Sampling Importance Resampling (SIR) ---
set.seed(20260929)

n_candidates_sir <- 10000
n_resample_sir <- 5000

# 1. Draw 10,000 proposal candidates from U(0, 1)
y_sir <- runif(n_candidates_sir)

# 2. Compute unnormalized weights w_i = f*(y_i) / g(y_i) [g(y) = 1]
weights_sir <- fstar(y_sir)

# 3. Resample 5,000 draws with replacement using normalized weights
sir_draws <- sample(y_sir, size = n_resample_sir, replace = TRUE, prob = weights_sir)
```

(c) Estimate $\E{X}$ from each sample, and check both against the exact
value from `integrate`.

```{r}
# --- (c) Estimate E[X] from both samples and compare against integrate() ---

# 1. Estimate E[X] from Monte Carlo samples
E_ar  <- mean(ar_draws)
E_sir <- mean(sir_draws)

# 2. Compute exact E[X] using R's integrate()
# E[X] = integral(x * f*(x)) / integral(f*(x))
num_int <- integrate(function(x) x * fstar(x), lower = 0, upper = 1)$value
den_int <- integrate(fstar, lower = 0, upper = 1)$value
E_exact <- num_int / den_int

# 3. Print side-by-side comparison
results <- tibble(
  Method = c("Exact (integrate)", "Accept-Reject", "Importance Resampling"),
  Estimate_E_X = c(E_exact, E_ar, E_sir),
  Sample_Size = c(NA, length(ar_draws), length(sir_draws))
)

print(results)
```


# Part D: Multivariate distributions and processes

## D.1

`faithful` records 272 eruptions of the Old Faithful geyser: the eruption
length and the waiting time to the next eruption, both in minutes.

```{r faithful}
ggplot(faithful, aes(x = eruptions, y = waiting)) + geom_point()
```

We model the pair as a mixture of two bivariate normals: with probability
$p$ a draw from $N_2(\mu_1, \Sigma_1)$, and otherwise a draw from
$N_2(\mu_2, \Sigma_2)$.

(a) Split the eruptions at 3 minutes. Estimate $p$ as the fraction of short
eruptions, and each component's mean and covariance from its group
(`colMeans`, `cov`).

```{r d1}
short <- faithful$eruptions < 3
p <- mean(short)
shortdf <- faithful[short, ]
longdf <- faithful[!short, ]
mu1 <- colMeans(faithful[short, ]);  S1 <- cov(faithful[short, ])
mu2 <- colMeans(faithful[!short, ]);  S2 <- cov(faithful[!short, ])

rmvn <- function(n, mu, Sigma) {
  C <- chol(Sigma)
  Z <- matrix(rnorm(2 * n), nrow = 2)
  t(mu + t(C) %*% Z)                # mu + C^T Z, one draw per column
}

simulated_lower <- rmvn(1000, mu1, S1)
ggplot(simulated_lower,
       aes(x = eruptions, y = waiting)) +
  geom_point()

rfaithful <- function(n) {
  n1 <- rbinom(1, n, p)                  # how many short eruptions
  x <- rbind(rmvn(n1, mu1, S1), rmvn(n - n1, mu2, S2))
  colnames(x) <- c("eruptions", "waiting")
  x
}

# your plot of the data next to rfaithful(272) here

p
mu1["waiting"]                           # mean wait after a short eruption
```

(b) Write `rfaithful(n)`, which draws from the fitted mixture. Generate each
normal component as $\mu + C^T Z$ with `C <- chol(Sigma)`, not with a package
function. Plot 272 simulated points next to the data.

```{r}
# 1. Generate 272 draws from the fitted mixture model
simulated_df <- as.data.frame(rfaithful(272)) %>% 
  mutate(Source = "Simulated (rfaithful)")

observed_df <- faithful %>% 
  mutate(Source = "Observed (faithful)")

# 2. Combine into a single data frame for side-by-side plotting
combined_df <- bind_rows(observed_df, simulated_df)

# 3. Create side-by-side scatter plots
ggplot(combined_df, aes(x = eruptions, y = waiting, color = Source)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ Source) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Observed (faithful)" = "#2b5c8f", 
                                "Simulated (rfaithful)" = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful Geyser: Observed Data vs. Mixture Simulation",
    x = "Eruption Duration (minutes)",
    y = "Waiting Time to Next Eruption (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## D.2

(a) Show that the mean of the mixture is $p \mu_1 + (1 - p) \mu_2$.

$$\E{X} = \E{WU} + \E{(1 - W)V} = \E{W}\,\E{U} + \E{(1-W)} \E{V} = 
p  \mu_1 + (1 - p) \mu_2$$

(b) Compare three covariance matrices: `cov(faithful)`, the covariance of
10,000 draws from `rfaithful`, and $p \Sigma_1 + (1 - p) \Sigma_2$. Is the
covariance of a mixture the weighted average of the component covariances?

```{r d2b}
cov(faithful)
cov(rfaithful(10000))
p * S1 + (1 - p) * S2
```

## D.3

`data/spy.rda` holds the daily closing price of SPY, a fund that tracks the
S&P 500, for 3,488 trading days from 2007 to 2020. Prices are adjusted for
dividends and splits.

```{r spy}
load("../../data/spy.rda")
logp <- log(spy$price)
r <- diff(logp)
ggplot(spy, aes(x = date, y = price)) + geom_line()
```

A simple model for the log price $L_t$ is a Gaussian random walk,
$L_t = L_{t-1} + \mu + \sigma Z_t$ with independent $Z_t \sim N(0, 1)$. Under
this model the daily log returns $r_t = L_t - L_{t-1}$ are independent
$N(\mu, \sigma^2)$.

(a) Estimate $\mu$ and $\sigma$ from the returns. Write `rwalk()`, which
simulates a log price path of the same length as the data from the fitted
walk, starting at the first observed $L_t$. Plot 20 simulated paths with the
observed one.

```{r}
# --- Part D.3(a): Return Estimation & Path Simulation ---
# 1. Calculate log returns and parameters
spy_prices <- spy$price
log_prices <- log(spy_prices)
r_t <- diff(log_prices)

n_days <- length(spy_prices)
mu_hat <- mean(r_t)
sigma_hat <- sd(r_t)

# Function to simulate a single random walk path
rwalk <- function(n, start_log_price, mu, sigma) {
  increments <- rnorm(n - 1, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
  c(start_log_price, start_log_price + cumsum(increments))
}

# 2. Simulate 20 paths
n_sims_plot <- 20
sim_paths <- replicate(n_sims_plot, rwalk(n_days, log_prices[1], mu_hat, sigma_hat))

# 3. Plot 20 simulated paths alongside actual SPY log prices
plot(1:n_days, log_prices, type = "l", col = "black", lwd = 2.5,
     ylim = range(c(log_prices, sim_paths)),
     xlab = "Trading Days", ylab = "Log(SPY Price)",
     main = "SPY Observed Log Prices vs. 20 Random Walk Simulations")

for (i in 1:n_sims_plot) {
  lines(1:n_days, sim_paths[, i], col = rgb(0.8, 0.2, 0.2, 0.3), lwd = 1.2)
}

legend("topleft", legend = c("Observed SPY", "Simulated Paths"),
       col = c("black", "red"), lwd = c(2.5, 1.2), bty = "n")
```


(b) The **largest drawdown** is the biggest fall from an earlier peak,
$\min_t \left(L_t - \max_{s \le t} L_s\right)$. `cummax` computes the running
peak. Compute the largest drawdown for the data, and give a Monte Carlo
$p$-value from 1,000 simulated paths. The alternative is that real
drawdowns are larger (more negative) than the model's.

```{r}
# --- Part D.3(b): Maximum Drawdown Test ---
max_drawdown <- function(L) {
  min(L - cummax(L))
}

# Observed statistic
D_obs <- max_drawdown(log_prices)

# Monte Carlo simulation (1,000 runs)
M_sims <- 1000
D_sims <- numeric(M_sims)

for (i in 1:M_sims) {
  path <- rwalk(n_days, log_prices[1], mu_hat, sigma_hat)
  D_sims[i] <- max_drawdown(path)
}

# Monte Carlo p-value for lower-tailed test (more negative drawdown)
p_val_drawdown <- mean(D_sims <= D_obs)

cat(sprintf("Observed Max Drawdown (Log Scale) : %.4f\n", D_obs))
cat(sprintf("Mean Simulated Max Drawdown        : %.4f\n", mean(D_sims)))
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo p-value (H1: D* <= D_obs): %.4f\n", p_val_drawdown))
```


(c) Repeat (b) with the correlation between $|r_t|$ and $|r_{t-1}|$ as the
statistic. It is large when big moves follow big moves. The alternative is
that it is larger than under the model.

```{r}
# --- Part D.3(c): Volatility Clustering Test ---
set.seed(20260929)

calc_vol_cluster <- function(returns) {
  cor(abs(returns[-1]), abs(returns[-length(returns)]))
}

# Observed statistic
C_obs <- calc_vol_cluster(r_t)

# Monte Carlo simulation (1,000 runs)
C_sims <- numeric(M_sims)

for (i in 1:M_sims) {
  sim_r <- rnorm(n_days - 1, mean = mu_hat, sd = sigma_hat)
  C_sims[i] <- calc_vol_cluster(sim_r)
}

# Monte Carlo p-value for upper-tailed test
p_val_vol <- mean(C_sims >= C_obs)

cat(sprintf("Observed Absolute Return Autocorrelation (C_obs) : %.4f\n", C_obs))
cat(sprintf("Mean Simulated Autocorrelation                    : %.4f\n", mean(C_sims)))
cat(sprintf("Monte Carlo p-value (H1: C* >= C_obs)             : %.4f\n", p_val_vol))
```


(d) Which feature of the data does the random walk reproduce, and which does
it miss?

**What the Random Walk Captures Well**: 

It effectively reproduces the overall trajectory (drift $\hat{\mu}$) and general volatility scale ($\hat{\sigma}$) of stock prices over long time horizons.

**Where the Random Walk Fails**:

Drawdown Severity: Real financial markets exhibit prolonged market crashes that produce significantly deeper drawdowns ($D_{\text{obs}}$) than expected under independent Gaussian returns.

Volatility Clustering: Real returns show significant positive autocorrelation in absolute returns ($C_{\text{obs}} > 0$), meaning quiet periods cluster together and high-volatility periods cluster together—a dynamic that the independent Gaussian model completely misses ($C^* \approx 0$).

# Part E: Gibbs sampling

A Morning Consult/Politico poll asked voters whether Congress should raise the
federal minimum wage. Leaving out those with no opinion:

```{r poll}
x1 <- 806  # raise it to $15/hr
x2 <- 435  # do not raise it
x3 <- 586  # raise it to $11/hr
```

We model the counts as multinomial with probabilities $\theta_1, \theta_2$ and
$\theta_3 = 1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2$:
$$f(x_1, x_2, x_3 \mid \theta_1, \theta_2) \propto
  \theta_1^{x_1} \theta_2^{x_2} (1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2)^{x_3}.$$
The prior is Dirichlet($\delta_1, \delta_2, \delta_3$), which generalizes the
Beta to three probabilities that sum to 1:
$$p(\theta_1, \theta_2) \propto
  \theta_1^{\delta_1 - 1} \theta_2^{\delta_2 - 1} (1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2)^{\delta_3 - 1}.$$

## E.1

(a) Show that the posterior is Dirichlet($x_1 + \delta_1, x_2 + \delta_2, x_3 + \delta_3$).

$$\theta_1^{x_1} \theta_2^{x_2} (1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2)^{x_3} \cdot
  \theta_1^{\delta_1 - 1} \theta_2^{\delta_2 - 1} (1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2)^{\delta_3 - 1}
  = \theta_1^{e_1 - 1}\, \theta_2^{e_2 - 1}\, (1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2)^{e_3 - 1}$$
  
$e_1 = x_1 + \delta_1$, $e_2 = x_2 + \delta_2$ and $e_3 = x_3 + \delta_3$

$$\pi(\theta_1, \theta_2 \mid x_1,
x_2, x_3) \propto \theta_1^{x_1 + \delta_1 - 1}\, 
\theta_2^{x_2 + \delta_2 - 1}\,
(1 - \theta_1 - \theta_2)^{x_3 + \delta_3 - 1}$$

(b) Show that the full conditional of $\theta_1$ is a scaled Beta,
$$\theta_1 \mid \theta_2, x \sim (1 - \theta_2) \, \text{Beta}(x_1 + \delta_1, \, x_3 + \delta_3),$$
and state the matching result for $\theta_2 \mid \theta_1, x$. Hint: if
$X = aB$ with $a > 0$, then $f_X(x) = f_B(x/a)/a$ (module 1 project, A.1).

Let $a_1 = x_1 + \delta_1$, $b = x_3 + \delta_3$ and $s = 1 - \theta_2$.
Keeping only the factors with $\theta_1$,
$\pi(\theta_1 \mid \theta_2, x) \propto \theta_1^{a_1 - 1} (s - \theta_1)^{b - 1}$
for $0 < \theta_1 < s$. For $B \sim \text{Beta}(a_1, b)$, the density of $sB$ is
$$\frac{1}{s} f_B\!\left(\frac{\theta_1}{s}\right) \propto
  \left(\frac{\theta_1}{s}\right)^{a_1 - 1} \left(1 - \frac{\theta_1}{s}\right)^{b - 1}
  \propto \text{(blank)}$$
  
$$\left(\frac{\theta_1}{s}\right)^{a_1 - 1} \left(s - \frac{\theta_1}{s}\right)^{b - 1}=
\left(\frac{\theta_1^{a_1-1}}{s^{a_1-1}}\right) \left(\frac{(s-\theta_1)^{b-1}}{s^{b-1}}\right)
\propto \theta_1^{a_1-1}(1-\theta_2-\theta_1)^{b-1}$$

## E.2

Write a Gibbs sampler that alternates the two full conditionals from E.1,
with every $\delta_i = 1$. Run 5,000 iterations starting from
$\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 1/3$, make a trace plot of $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$,
and discard the first 1,000. Report the posterior mean and a 95% credible
interval (the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the draws) for $\theta_1$,
$\theta_2$ and $\theta_3$, and estimate $P(\theta_1 / \theta_2 > 2 \mid x)$.

```{r e2}
gibbs <- function(k, t1 = 1/3, t2 = 1/3) {
  chain <- matrix(0, k, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("theta1", "theta2")))
  for (i in 1:k) {
    t1 <- (1 - t2) * rbeta(1, x1 + 1, x3 + 1)
    t2 <- (1 - t1) * rbeta(1, x2 + 1, x3 + 1)
    chain[i, ] <- c(t1, t2)
  }
  chain
}
chain <- gibbs(5000)
matplot(chain, type = "l", lty = 1)          # trace plot
post <- chain[-(1:1000), ]
post <- cbind(post, theta3 = 1 - post[, "theta1"] - post[, "theta2"])
rbind(mean = colMeans(post), apply(post, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975)))
mean(post[, "theta1"] / post[, "theta2"] > 2)
```

## E.3

If $G_1, G_2, G_3$ are independent with $G_i \sim \text{Gamma}(a_i, 1)$, then
$(G_1, G_2, G_3) / (G_1 + G_2 + G_3)$ is Dirichlet($a_1, a_2, a_3$). With two
components this is the Beta: $G_1 / (G_1 + G_2) \sim \text{Beta}(a_1, a_2)$.

The same construction gives the marginal posterior of $\theta_1$. Write
$\theta_1 = G_1 / (G_1 + H)$ with $H = G_2 + G_3$. A sum of independent
gammas with the same rate is gamma, so $H \sim \text{Gamma}(a_2 + a_3, 1)$,
independent of $G_1$, and therefore
$\theta_1 \mid x \sim \text{Beta}(a_1, a_2 + a_3)$.

Both results involve a Beta, but they are different distributions:

| | distribution | used by |
|---|---|---|
| full conditional $\theta_1 \mid \theta_2, x$ | $(1 - \theta_2)\,\text{Beta}(a_1, a_3)$ | the Gibbs sampler in E.2 |
| marginal $\theta_1 \mid x$ | $\text{Beta}(a_1, a_2 + a_3)$ | the check below |

The conditional depends on the current value of $\theta_2$, and the marginal
does not. The Gibbs sampler needs only the conditionals. We use the marginal
here to check the chain.

Draw 4,000 values from the posterior directly with the gamma construction.
Make QQ plots of the direct draws of $\theta_1$ and of the Gibbs draws of
$\theta_1$ against the Beta($a_1, a_2 + a_3$) quantile function (`qbeta`, with
the shape parameters passed through `dparams` as in A.2), and compare
the two estimates of $P(\theta_1 / \theta_2 > 2 \mid x)$.

```{r}
# =============================================================================
# PART E.3: Validation of Gibbs Sampler via Direct Gamma Sampling
# =============================================================================

# Define posterior hyper-parameters vector 'a' (with prior delta = (1, 1, 1))
a <- c(x1 + 1, x2 + 1, x3 + 1)

# Generate 4,000 direct draws using Gamma construction
set.seed(20260929)
n_direct <- 4000
g1 <- rgamma(n_direct, shape = a[1], rate = 1)
g2 <- rgamma(n_direct, shape = a[2], rate = 1)
g3 <- rgamma(n_direct, shape = a[3], rate = 1)

g_sum <- g1 + g2 + g3
direct <- cbind(
  theta1 = g1 / g_sum,
  theta2 = g2 / g_sum,
  theta3 = g3 / g_sum
)

# --- Part E.3(a): Q-Q Plots using geom_qq with dparams -----------------------

shape1_param <- a[1]
shape2_param <- a[2] + a[3]

# Data frame combining direct and Gibbs draws for ggplot
qq_df <- bind_rows(
  tibble(theta1 = direct[, "theta1"], Method = "Direct Gamma Sampling"),
  tibble(theta1 = post[, "theta1"],   Method = "Gibbs Sampler")
)

ggplot(qq_df, aes(sample = theta1)) +
  geom_qq(
    distribution = qbeta,
    dparams = list(shape1 = shape1_param, shape2 = shape2_param),
    color = "#2b5c8f",
    alpha = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_qq_line(
    distribution = qbeta,
    dparams = list(shape1 = shape1_param, shape2 = shape2_param),
    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Method) +
  labs(
    title = "Q-Q Plot of theta1 Draws vs. Theoretical Beta(a1, a2 + a3)",
    x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
    y = "Sample Quantiles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# --- Part E.3(b): Comparative Posterior Probability P(theta1 / theta2 > 2 | x)

prob_direct <- mean((direct[, "theta1"] / direct[, "theta2"]) > 2)
prob_gibbs  <- mean((post[, "theta1"] / post[, "theta2"]) > 2)

results_e3 <- tibble(
  Method = c("Direct Gamma Draws", "Gibbs Sampler"),
  P_Theta1_gt_2Theta2 = c(prob_direct, prob_gibbs)
)

print(results_e3)
```
